title: Discrete Mathematics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Discrete Mathematics curriculum: propositional and predicate logic, proof techniques, relations and functions, graph theory (Eulerian/Hamiltonian graphs, trees, graph coloring), combinatorics and the pigeonhole principle, recurrence relations, Boolean algebra, and an introduction to algorithmic complexity.

questions.question: In propositional logic, the statement p → q (p implies q) is false only when:
options: p is true and q is false
p is false and q is true
both p and q are false
both p and q are true
questions.correct_answer: p is true and q is false
questions.explanation: A conditional statement p→q is false in exactly one case: when the hypothesis p is true but the conclusion q is false.

questions.question: The logical statement ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent, by De Morgan's Law, to:
questions.correct_answer: ¬p ∨ ¬q
questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law states the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations: ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q.

questions.question: A statement that is always true, regardless of the truth values of its components, is called a:
questions.correct_answer: tautology
questions.explanation: A tautology is a compound statement that evaluates to true under every possible assignment of truth values, such as p ∨ ¬p.

questions.question: The converse of the statement 'if p then q' is:
options: if not p then not q
if not q then not p
questions.correct_answer: if q then p
questions.explanation: The converse swaps the hypothesis and conclusion of the original conditional statement.

questions.question: The contrapositive of 'if p then q' is 'if not q then not p'. The contrapositive is:
options: logically equivalent to the original statement
the opposite of the original statement
never true when the original is true
questions.correct_answer: logically equivalent to the original statement
questions.explanation: A conditional statement and its contrapositive always have identical truth values, making proof by contrapositive a valid technique.

questions.question: In predicate logic, the statement ∀x P(x) is read as:
options: for all x, P(x) is true
there exists an x such that P(x) is true
P is a function of x
questions.correct_answer: for all x, P(x) is true
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier ∀ asserts that the predicate P(x) holds for every element x in the domain of discourse.

questions.question: The negation of ∀x P(x) is:
questions.correct_answer: ∃x ¬P(x)
questions.explanation: Negating a universal statement produces an existential statement of the negated predicate: ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).

questions.question: A proof by contradiction begins by:
options: assuming the negation of the statement to be proved and deriving a logical inconsistency
assuming the statement is true and stopping
questions.correct_answer: assuming the negation of the statement to be proved and deriving a logical inconsistency
questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of the desired conclusion, then shows this assumption leads to a contradiction, forcing the original statement to be true.

questions.question: Proof by mathematical induction consists of proving a base case and then proving:
options: that if the statement holds for n = k, it holds for n = k+1
the statement for every n individually
the statement is false for large n
questions.correct_answer: that if the statement holds for n = k, it holds for n = k+1
questions.explanation: The inductive step shows the truth of the statement propagates from any k to k+1, which combined with the base case proves it for all n in the domain.

questions.question: A relation R on a set A is called reflexive if:
questions.correct_answer: (a,a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A
questions.explanation: Reflexivity requires every element to be related to itself.

questions.question: A relation R on a set A is called symmetric if:
questions.correct_answer: (a,b) ∈ R implies (b,a) ∈ R
questions.explanation: Symmetry means the relation is order-independent: if a is related to b, then b must also be related to a.

questions.question: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive is called an:
questions.correct_answer: equivalence relation
questions.explanation: A relation satisfying all three properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) is an equivalence relation, which partitions the set into equivalence classes.

questions.question: A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive is called a:
questions.correct_answer: partial order relation
questions.explanation: Partial orders satisfy reflexivity, antisymmetry (a R b and b R a implies a = b), and transitivity, generalizing the ≤ relation.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is called injective (one-to-one) if:
options: distinct elements of A map to distinct elements of B
every element of B has a preimage
A and B have the same size
questions.correct_answer: distinct elements of A map to distinct elements of B
questions.explanation: Injectivity requires that f(a1) = f(a2) implies a1 = a2, i.e., no two distinct inputs share the same output.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is called surjective (onto) if:
options: every element of B is the image of at least one element of A
A is a subset of B
f(a) is unique for each a
questions.correct_answer: every element of B is the image of at least one element of A
questions.explanation: Surjectivity requires the range of f to be all of B, meaning every element in the codomain has at least one preimage.

questions.question: A function that is both injective and surjective is called:
questions.correct_answer: bijective
questions.explanation: A bijective function establishes a one-to-one correspondence between A and B, and is invertible.

questions.question: In a simple undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is defined as:
options: the number of edges incident to that vertex
the total number of vertices in the graph
the shortest path length from that vertex
questions.correct_answer: the number of edges incident to that vertex
questions.explanation: The degree of a vertex counts how many edges are directly connected to it.

questions.question: By the Handshaking Lemma, the sum of all vertex degrees in a graph equals:
questions.correct_answer: twice the number of edges
questions.explanation: Since every edge contributes exactly 2 to the total degree count (one for each endpoint), the sum of degrees is always 2|E|.

questions.question: A graph has an Eulerian circuit (a closed walk using every edge exactly once) if and only if:
options: every vertex has even degree and the graph is connected
questions.correct_answer: every vertex has even degree and the graph is connected
questions.explanation: Euler's theorem states a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree.

questions.question: A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is a cycle that:
options: visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start
questions.correct_answer: visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start
questions.explanation: A Hamiltonian cycle is a closed path that passes through every vertex of the graph exactly once before returning to the starting vertex.

questions.question: A tree, in graph theory, is defined as:
options: a connected graph with no cycles
a graph with all vertices of degree 2
questions.correct_answer: a connected graph with no cycles
questions.explanation: A tree is a connected, acyclic graph; a graph with a tree structure in each of its components (allowing disconnection) is called a forest.

questions.question: A tree with n vertices always has exactly:
questions.correct_answer: n - 1 edges
questions.explanation: This is a fundamental property of trees: a connected acyclic graph on n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges.

questions.question: The chromatic number of a graph is defined as:
options: the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so no two adjacent vertices share a color
the number of edges in the graph
questions.correct_answer: the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so no two adjacent vertices share a color
questions.explanation: The chromatic number χ(G) is the smallest number of colors required for a proper vertex coloring of the graph.

questions.question: By the Four Color Theorem, every planar graph can be properly vertex-colored using at most:
options: n colors, where n is the number of vertices
questions.correct_answer: 4 colors
questions.explanation: The Four Color Theorem states that any planar graph's vertices (regions of a map) can be colored with no more than four colors such that no two adjacent regions share a color.

questions.question: The Pigeonhole Principle states that if n items are placed into m containers with n > m, then:
options: at least one container must contain more than one item
each container has exactly one item
questions.correct_answer: at least one container must contain more than one item
questions.explanation: This basic counting principle guarantees a collision when more items than containers are distributed among them.

questions.question: The Pigeonhole Principle can be used to prove that among any 13 people, at least two:
questions.correct_answer: share the same birth month
questions.explanation: With 13 people and only 12 months, by the pigeonhole principle at least two people must share a birth month.

questions.question: A recurrence relation defines a sequence by:
options: expressing each term as a function of one or more previous terms
giving an explicit closed formula only
questions.correct_answer: expressing each term as a function of one or more previous terms
questions.explanation: A recurrence relation recursively defines later terms in terms of earlier ones, such as the Fibonacci relation Fn = Fn-1 + Fn-2.

questions.question: For the Fibonacci recurrence Fn = Fn-1 + Fn-2 with F0=0, F1=1, the value of F5 is:
questions.explanation: Computing terms: F2=1, F3=2, F4=3, F5=5.

questions.question: A linear homogeneous recurrence relation with constant coefficients, an = c1 an-1 + c2 an-2, is typically solved using:
questions.correct_answer: the characteristic (auxiliary) equation method
questions.explanation: This mirrors the method for constant-coefficient linear ODEs: assuming an = r^n leads to a characteristic polynomial whose roots determine the general solution.

questions.question: In Boolean algebra, the expression A + A'B simplifies to:
questions.correct_answer: A + B
questions.explanation: Using the absorption/distribution identity, A + A'B = A + B, a standard Boolean algebra simplification.

questions.question: In Boolean algebra, De Morgan's Laws state that (A·B)' equals:
questions.correct_answer: A' + B'
questions.explanation: De Morgan's Law for Boolean algebra: the complement of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the complements.

questions.question: In algorithmic complexity, Big-O notation O(n^2) describes an algorithm whose running time:
options: grows proportionally to the square of the input size, for large n
is constant regardless of input size
questions.correct_answer: grows proportionally to the square of the input size, for large n
questions.explanation: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound; O(n^2) means the running time is bounded above by a constant multiple of n^2 for sufficiently large n.

questions.question: Between an algorithm with time complexity O(n log n) and one with O(n^2), for very large n:
options: the O(n log n) algorithm will eventually run faster
the O(n^2) algorithm always runs faster
they always take the same time
questions.correct_answer: the O(n log n) algorithm will eventually run faster
questions.explanation: Since n log n grows more slowly than n^2 as n increases, the O(n log n) algorithm becomes faster for sufficiently large inputs.
